The long road of the Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci from Macau, where he landed in 1582, to the court of the Ming emperor in Beijing, which he entered in 1601. It began the first lasting Christian mission inside China in modern times.

Ricci and his fellow Jesuit Michele Ruggieri settled in Zhaoqing in 1583. Ricci mastered classical Chinese, dressed first as a Buddhist monk and then as a scholar, and argued that Christianity fitted Confucian ethics. He won over officials with clocks, prisms and a world map in Chinese that showed the Americas.

In Beijing the Wanli Emperor let him stay, though the two never met. With the scholar and convert Xu Guangqi he translated the first six books of Euclid's Elements into Chinese. He died there in 1610 and was buried in ground granted by the emperor.

His habit of adapting to Chinese custom kept Jesuits at court into the Qing and the reign of the Kangxi Emperor. It also led to the bitter Chinese Rites controversy in the Catholic Church.
